big_idea: We can TEST a prediction in a new group. The same prediction may give DIFFERENT results.
learning_intention: We are learning to test a prediction in a new group.
student_learning_goal: I can test a prediction in a new group.
success_criteria: I can MAKE a prediction in one group.
I can TEST the same prediction in a different group.
I can compare the two results.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Lucky and Mae — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Lesson 4 test tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Mae: I predicted MOST kids in our class like dogs. Now I'll TEST in Ms. B's class — same numbers? Or different? Mae opens: 'Different group? Different data — that is OK!' (Class echoes.)
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Lucky and Mae puppets. 'Friends — yesterday we PREDICTED. Today we TEST predictions in a NEW group to see if results are the SAME.'

Introduce vocabulary. Write TEST on chart. 'Test = try the prediction in a new group, count what happens.'

Demonstrate. Show class data. 'Yesterday I asked our class: dog, cat, fish? 12 dogs, 6 cats, 2 fish. Most chose DOG.'

'Today I PREDICT — Ms. B's class will also pick dog the most. Let's TEST.'

Show Ms. B's hypothetical data. '8 dogs, 9 cats, 3 fish. CATS most! Different from us.'

Generalise. 'Lucky says — predictions can be RIGHT for one group and WRONG for another. Different groups can have different favourites.'

More examples:
- Predict: 'Most kids in school like sunny weather.' Test in Grade 2 class. Compare.
- Predict: 'Most pets are dogs.' Test in family survey. Compare.
- Predict: 'Most kids walked to school today.' Test in another class. Compare.

'Mae says — testing is HONEST. We accept the results, even if they don't match our prediction.'

'Today YOU predict and test predictions across groups.'

steps.instruction: Whole group: predict 'most kids in our class like ___' for 4 categories. Then a teacher-aide brings results from another G1 class to compare.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say: 'Predict for our class. Now compare with another class.'

steps.instruction: Three stations. Station A: Re-coin Pull — bag with 4 red + 1 blue. Predict 5 pulls. Then test with the bag of 1 red + 4 blue. Compare. Station B: Pet survey — predict for family, test for friend. Station C: Weather — predict tomorrow, test what actually happens.
Stretch challenge at Station B: predict for 2 groups (family + friend) and compare ALL.
Discuss outcome variability. 'Same prediction, different group, DIFFERENT results. That's OK!'
steps.teacher_prompt: Show: red-bag pulls vs blue-bag pulls.

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the test tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Ask 'Was the prediction right in this group?' Mark the tracker.

steps.instruction: STRATEGY COMPARE: Two pairs share their mismatched test results (7R/3B vs 8R/2B). Class debates: which is RIGHT? Resolution — both, because the underlying ratio (4:1) is expressed differently across small samples. Cite Konold & Pollatsek (2002) signal-vs-noise framing.
steps.teacher_prompt: Mae: 'Same bag, different test, different counts. The math trick is to LOOK PAST the wiggles and see the pattern.'

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay at Station A with the bag-pull only. Skip prediction reasoning.
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch at Station B: 2-group comparison + reason.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide sentence frame: 'In group 1, ___ was most. In group 2, ___ was most.'
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Children walk between two simulated 'classrooms' (corners of the room) for testing.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: makes prediction; tests in new group; compares results.

discussion_prompts: Were any predictions WRONG in another group?
Why might different groups have different results?
What does this tell us about predictions?
consolidation.exit_routine: Mae's variability refrain — class chants 3x: 'Different group? Different data — that is OK!' Then Lucky reminds: 'I predict and I PROVE!' Each child reports their pair's data and sticks the result onto the class pooled chart.

assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 4 captures D2.2 mastery for testing predictions across populations.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child insists their prediction was right despite different test results — repairing the prediction-stuck trap at Grade 1
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
Across pairs/groups, test results VARY — even with the same setup, two pairs running 10 pulls of a 4R+1B bag may report 7R/3B vs 8R/2B. The G1 trap is to interpret this as 'someone is wrong.' Konold & Pollatsek (2002, 'Data Analysis as the Search for Signals in Noisy Processes') frame this as the foundation of variability literacy — the SIGNAL (probability) is constant; the data are noisy.

Yesterday Lucky predicted (Lesson 3). Today we test and reconcile across pairs. Tomorrow's capstone (Lesson 5) integrates the full likelihood-prediction-test loop.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station B. Child predicted family pets favourite = 'dog'. Tested with a friend's family — favourite was 'cat'. Child says 'but my prediction was right because in MY family it's dogs'.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'You're partly right — in YOUR family, dogs were most. But the TEST asks about THIS group, not your family.'

Walk through. 'A prediction is for ONE group. When we TEST in a NEW group, we accept the new group's results.'

Generalise. 'Lucky says — predictions don't COVER all groups. Each group can be different. The same prediction can be right or wrong depending on the group.'

Now re-frame. 'For your family: dogs most (RIGHT for your family). For your friend's family: cats most (DIFFERENT — that's their data).'

If still stuck: show 3 different groups with different favourites. 'See — the same question gives 3 different answers.' Force the variability acceptance.

Long-term recovery: every test cycle names BOTH groups and accepts both results.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Insists prediction was right despite different test.
(Mid) Accepts that test result is for new group, with prompts.
(Strong) Independently names that predictions can vary by group.
(Stretched) Predicts FOR each group separately and reasons about why they differ.
common_misconceptions: My prediction works for everyone. (Repair: predictions are group-specific.)
If I'm right once, I'm right always. (Repair: same prediction can be wrong in another group.)
Different results = data is bad. (Repair: different results = different groups, that's expected.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child says 'someone is wrong' when pairs report different results: lay both result sheets side-by-side, note both are 'mostly red' even if exact counts differ. Variability is normal.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child wants to redo the test until results match: drill 'we keep ALL the data, even when it varies. The pattern is what we trust.'
DIAGNOSTIC C — child cannot articulate the pattern across pairs: make a class chart pooling every pair's results, count totals, show the underlying ratio (~4:1) emerges from the pooled data.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of D2.2 testing predictions.

parts_outline.task: Look at our class data. Predict for ANOTHER class. Then look at the other class data. Right or wrong?
Test 2 predictions: pet preference at home vs school. Record both.
Write WHY predictions can be different in different groups.
